props.title: The Thomas Crown Affair
props.initialSlug: Millionaire playboy plots perfect heist to outwit cops

sections.content: The Thomas Crown Affair revolutionized the heist film genre through Steve McQueen's sophisticated portrayal of a bored millionaire orchestrating bank robberies for sport. Director Norman Jewison employed revolutionary split-screen techniques that turned mundane scenes into visual puzzles, influencing films like Ocean's Eleven (2001) and Inside Man (2006). The cat-and-mouse romance between McQueen and Faye Dunaway's insurance investigator created a template for sexy crime capers, later seen in films like Out of Sight (1998) and The Score (2001).

sections.content: The film's influence on fashion and style cannot be overstated. McQueen's three-piece suits and Dunaway's Vogue-worthy wardrobe by Theadora Van Runkle set trends that echo through films like Casino Royale (2006) and Inception (2010). The chess scene between Crown and Vickers remains one of cinema's most erotically charged non-physical encounters, inspiring similar tension-filled moments in Basic Instinct (1992) and The Usual Suspects (1995). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Technical Innovation

Michel Legrand's Oscar-winning song "The Windmills of Your Mind" established a new standard for sophisticated crime film soundtracks, influencing composers like David Holmes (Ocean's Eleven series) and Hans Zimmer (The Dark Knight (2008)). Jewison's innovative use of split-screen techniques, particularly during the heist sequences, influenced directors like Brian De Palma (Sisters (1972)) and Quentin Tarantino (Jackie Brown (1997)).
